nature-acct-116.title: World Happiness Report: ranking nations by how people rate their lives
nature-acct-116.text: Colombia ranked 37th in 2018, yet first on Gallup's Positive Experience Index. The gap shows what the World Happiness Report measures. This annual publication ranks national happiness from people's own ratings of their lives. Rankings rest on one life-evaluation question, the Cantril ladder, in which respondents rate their current life from 0 (worst) to 10 (best), with data mainly from the Gallup World Poll. Six factors, such as GDP per capita and social support, are compared with a hypothetical nation, Dystopia, but they do not change a country's total, and they show correlation, not causation. The report grew out of UN General Assembly resolution 65/309 (2011); the first appeared in April 2012. Whether single-item and multi-item scales best measure life satisfaction is still debated. It builds on {{ref:nature-acct-019}}.

nature-acct-119.title: Net domestic product: GDP after the machines wear out
nature-acct-119.text:
A country can raise its output by spending more on replacing worn-out machines, and be no better off. Net domestic product (NDP) is gross domestic product minus the depreciation of a country's capital goods. It accounts for capital consumed during the year, such as the wearing out of housing, vehicles and machinery. The amount deducted is often called the capital consumption allowance, the amount needed to replace the depreciated assets.

Investment that only replaces worn-out equipment keeps output up but adds nothing to the economy's capacity, so rising GDP from higher replacement spending would not make anyone better off. Some economists therefore see NDP as a better measure of social and economic well-being. A growing gap between GDP and NDP signals increasing obsolescence of capital goods; a narrowing gap means the capital stock is improving. NDP adjusted for resource depletion, called EDP, was proposed as a green alternative but was not formally included in the System of National Accounts.

nature-acct-118.title: Supply chains: tiers behind the product
nature-acct-118.text: A supply chain is the system of facilities that turn raw materials into finished products and distribute them to end customers. Suppliers sit in tiers: first-tier suppliers serve the client directly, second-tier suppliers serve the first tier, and so on. After the 2013 Savar building collapse, auditing had to reach past first-tier suppliers, with better visibility and local partnerships. The EU's draft supply chain law sets due diligence requirements to protect human rights and the environment along the chain. Resilience has been read as persistence, then as adaptation and transformation, treating the chain as a social-ecological system.

nature-pol-294.title: Waste incineration: burning rubbish for heat
nature-pol-294.text:
Burn a tonne of municipal waste and about a tonne of CO2 goes up the stack. Incineration is a waste treatment process that burns the substances in waste, turning it into ash, flue gas and heat. Nearly all the carbon in the waste leaves as CO2. Plants come in several designs, such as moving grate, fixed grate, rotary-kiln and fluidised bed; the moving grate is typical for {{ref:nature-pol-064}}.

Heat can raise steam to drive a turbine. Net output is about 2/3 MWh of electricity and 2 MWh of district heating per tonne of municipal waste. Raw flue gas can carry {{ref:nature-pol-068}}, heavy metals, dioxins, furans, sulfur dioxide and hydrochloric acid, so modern plants add flue gas cleaning.

Ash makes up 4 to 10% of the waste by volume and 15-20% by weight. Fly ash is about 10-20% of it, and bottom ash can go to {{ref:nature-pol-058}} or be recycled as construction aggregate. Plant lifetimes of 25 to 30 years and the long contracts needed to recover investment can lock a municipality in.

nature-pol-296.title: Black carbon: the soot that warms and kills
nature-pol-296.text:
Black carbon is the light-absorbing form of elemental carbon left by pyrolysis or produced by incomplete combustion, as in soot. It forms from incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuel and biomass and is fine {{ref:nature-pol-068}} that causes premature death and disability. About 20% of emissions come from biofuels, 40% from fossil fuels and 40% from open biomass burning.

Developed countries were once the main source, but control technologies since the 1950s shifted most emissions to developing countries. Estimates say 640,000 to 4,900,000 premature deaths a year could be prevented with available mitigation measures. In soils black carbon is typically 1 to 6% of organic carbon, and Terra preta soils hold about three times the organic matter of surrounding soils.

nature-pol-299.title: Environmental remediation: cleaning up contaminated land
nature-pol-299.text:
Before a polluted site can be reused, someone has to clean it. Environmental remediation is the removal, treatment or containment of hazardous substances in soil, groundwater and sediment. Assessment begins when a site is suspected contaminated, often with a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment guided by the site's history. Waste can be removed and transported off-site for disposal, or contained by physical barriers such as slurry walls.

Regulations may require remediation before land is redeveloped, and voluntary cleanups can earn incentives, such as New York State's Brownfield Cleanup Program. Cleanup standards differ: the US uses EPA Regional Screening Levels, Europe has the Dutch standards, and Canadian provinces set their own. In the US a tax on polluting industries funds a Superfund for abandoned sites. Elsewhere sites are often rezoned to higher uses so land value covers cleanup costs. Remediation can face local resistance to rezoning; main impacts are noise, dust, odour and incremental health risk.

nature-pol-295.title: The incineration debate
nature-pol-295.text: Few waste plants divide a neighborhood like an incinerator. Using them for waste management weighs the economic appeal of local industry against health and environmental risk. Supporters say {{ref:nature-pol-294}} avoids landfill methane, saves landfill space where land is scarce, and replaces fossil power with partly biomass-based energy. They also note that in Europe the highest incineration rates generally go with top recycling performance. Critics say fly ash concentrates ecotoxic heavy metals and needs specialized landfills, and that the waste hierarchy prefers prevention, reuse and recycling. In the UK, the EU Landfill Directive led to the landfill tax and the Landfill Allowance Trading Scheme. Business, regulators, activists and residents contest it over health, recycling and lock-in.

nature-pol-297.title: Black carbon and the climate
nature-pol-297.text: Black carbon warms the climate by absorbing sunlight, altering clouds and darkening snow and ice. The IPCC's 2007 report put direct forcing from fossil-fuel black carbon at +0.2 W/m2 and the snow and ice albedo effect at an additional +0.1 W/m2. Later estimates rank it second after carbon dioxide. Estimates of direct forcing range from the IPCC's +0.34 W/m2 (plus or minus 0.25) to 0.9 W/m2 by Ramanathan and Carmichael. Because it stays in the air only weeks, cutting emissions may be the fastest way to slow near-term warming. A 2013 study found gas flares contributed over 40% of black carbon deposited in the Arctic.

nature-pol-298.title: Cutting black carbon with technology we already have
nature-pol-298.text: Black carbon can be cut with existing technology and national laws on particulate emissions. Developed nations reduced fossil-fuel black carbon by a factor of 5 or more since 1950, mainly to improve air quality and public health. Small-scale sources such as domestic cooking may shift when affordable alternatives exist, while vehicles and coal boilers may need regulation. Policy options include regulating slash-and-burn clearing, shore power for ships at port, and vehicle emissions tests with retrofitting such as particulate traps.

nature-pol-301.title: Incremental health risk: how much added danger is acceptable
nature-pol-301.text: Cleaning a site, or leaving it dirty, adds some risk for the people nearby. Incremental health risk is that added risk, whether from a remediation project or from the lack of one. It rests on carcinogenic and other effects and involves value judgements about the acceptable projected rate of increase in cancer. The acceptable increase is 1 in 1,000,000 in some jurisdictions and 1 in 100,000 in others.

nature-pol-300.title: Remediation technologies: treating contamination in place or out of it
nature-pol-300.text: Remediation technologies fall into two groups. Ex-situ methods excavate or extract contaminated soil and groundwater for surface treatment; in-situ methods treat contamination in place. Pump and treat draws up contaminated groundwater and purifies it, for petroleum usually through granular activated carbon. In situ chemical oxidation injects strong oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide, ozone, potassium permanganate or persulfates. Stabilization and solidification binds contaminants to stop their mobility, but has durability problems and cement CO2 emissions. Bioremediation uses microorganisms, through biostimulation, bioaugmentation or natural attenuation, in situ or ex situ. Nanoremediation uses nano-sized reactive agents that degrade organic contaminants or immobilize metals such as lead or arsenic.

nature-pol-302.title: Greenfield land: building on undeveloped ground
nature-pol-302.text: Greenfield land is undeveloped land, farmed, landscaped or left natural, in an urban or rural area. It is usually agricultural or amenity land being considered for urban development, and gives a developer high freedom compared with built-up sites. A developer may instead redevelop brownfield or greyfield land that was built on but left abandoned or underused.

nature-pol-303.title: Biofuel: fuel grown in a season
nature-pol-303.text:
Biofuel is made over a short time span from biomass, rather than by the very slow natural processes that form fossil fuels. It can come from plants or from agricultural, domestic or industrial bio waste, and is mostly used for transport but also for heating and electricity. It is regarded as a renewable energy source, yet it faces criticism over the food-versus-fuel debate, varied sustainability assessments, and {{ref:nature-eco-053}} and {{ref:nature-eco-035}} from production.

Global production was 81 Mtoe in 2017, about 3% a year above 2010. The US led with 37 Mtoe, then Brazil and South America at 23 Mtoe and Europe at 12 Mtoe. Emissions are not inherently carbon-neutral: they depend on feedstock, processing, transport and land-use change, and range from -127.1 gCO2eq per MJ with carbon capture to above 95 gCO2eq per MJ where land-use change is large. EU and UK policies require biofuels to deliver at least 65% greenhouse gas savings against fossil fuels (70% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin). The International Resource Panel concluded that biofuels differ in their effects on climate, energy security and ecosystems, so effects should be assessed over the whole life cycle.

nature-pol-311.title: Urban sprawl: cities that spread and spread
nature-pol-311.text:
Researchers admit the term lacks precision. Urban sprawl is the rapid spread of cities and towns, often with low-density housing, single-use zoning and heavy reliance on the private car: unrestricted spread of housing, commerce and roads over large areas with little concern for dense urban planning. Single-use development separates homes, work, shops and recreation so far that walking, transit and cycling are impractical and every activity needs a car. It builds on {{ref:nature-pol-177}}.

Sprawl often takes fertile farmland next to cities, and in the US a like-kind exchange tax break means the tax code subsidizes it. Environmental effects include land consumption, habitat loss, lower biodiversity and local ecosystem destruction; a review found urbanization endangers more US species than any other human activity. Lost habitat and fragmentation raise contact between wildlife and people, which can raise vector-borne and zoonotic disease risk.

Sprawl raises driving, vehicle emissions and air pollution, cuts physical activity, and raises crash risk through greater exposure to driving. Public services cost more in spread-out areas: roads, pipes, sewers and power lines are longer per household, so maintenance costs more.

nature-pol-308.title: Food versus fuel: crops for cars or for plates
nature-pol-308.text: Should farmland grow fuel or food? Biofuel production can compete with food crops. The text says a 50% cut in grain used for biofuels in the US and Europe would replace all of Ukraine's grain exports. Second- and third-generation biofuels use feedstocks that do not directly compete with food or feed crops, such as wastes and residues, to avoid the dilemma. Yet second-generation fuels raise competition for lignocellulosic biomass and so its cost. Responsible policies and economic instruments are needed to make {{ref:nature-pol-303}} production sustainable. Sources flag the food-versus-fuel question as contested.

nature-pol-309.title: Indirect land use change: the emissions biofuels cause elsewhere
nature-pol-309.text:
A biofuel can look clean at the field and dirty on the far side of the world. Indirect land use change is the unintended extra carbon emissions from land-use change elsewhere, caused by cropland expanding to meet global demand for {{ref:nature-pol-303}}. Farmers worldwide respond to higher crop prices by clearing pristine land to replace the food crops diverted to biofuel. Because rainforests and {{ref:nature-eco-467}} store carbon, clearing them raises net greenhouse gas emissions. Some authors argue it also affects biodiversity, water quality, food prices and supply, land tenure, worker migration and community stability.

Before 2008, life-cycle studies found corn, cellulosic and Brazilian sugarcane ethanol cut emissions versus gasoline, but none counted these effects. A 2008 Searchinger paper concluded that indirect effects offset the direct gains of corn and cellulosic ethanol. Payback was 4 years for Brazilian sugarcane, 167 for US corn and 52 for cellulosic ethanol, over a 30-year horizon. Critics such as Wang and Haq called the assumptions outdated, and Searchinger replied that ignoring these emissions is wrong however hard they are to predict.

The size of the emissions was disputed by the studies' authors and critics. In 2009 the California Air Resources Board included indirect land use change in the California Low-Carbon Fuel Standard, in force in 2011. A 2010 Brazil study projected indirect deforestation of 121,970 km2 by 2020 from sugarcane ethanol and soybean biodiesel, a carbon debt taking about 250 years to repay.

nature-pol-306.title: Aviation biofuel: greener jet fuel
nature-pol-306.text: Aviation biofuel, also called bio-jet fuel or sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), is a biofuel for aircraft. The International Air Transport Association regards it as a key way to cut aviation's environmental impact. As a drop-in replacement it needs no major aircraft engine changes, so it can decarbonize hard-to-abate medium and long-haul flights.
